catalog_quote: 2. 4 Syllable and mora. The syllable structure is generally represented as (C)V(V)(C), where the parenthesized elements are optional. ... A syllable can further be divided into moras, which consist of a primary mora (= Pm below) and additional secondary moras (= Sm): (C)V = Pm, (V) = Sm, (C) = Sm. The division into moras is valid for the formulation of pitch accent (see 2. 6). Any word consists of at least two moras, and monosyllabic words always contain VV. ... 2. 6 Pitch accent. The accent is fixed and therefore non-phonemic in Uilta. The penultimate mora (if it is the secondary mora, then the preceding primary mora) of a word is pronounced in the highest pitch and therefore can be called the accent peak. Except for the words which have the accent peak on the first mora, the high pitch begins with the second mora and is maintained up to the accent peak. The following is an example of …

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote verified verbatim in the held Tsumagari 2009 PDF/txt at sec. 2.4 (p.3) and sec. 2.6 (pp.3-4). (2) The classification rests on a 2009 grammar sketch, but by the language's principal specialist summarising his own dedicated 1983 accent study; a repository and catalogue sweep (TUFS, HUSCAP via CiNii/IRDB, CiNii 97 hits, Cambridge Core/JIPA, Crossref) found no instrumental or competing phonological analysis. (3) Three Glottolog-listed or related works were fetched sources openly and read: Yamada 2017 repeats the identical penultimate-mora pitch-accent rule for the Northern dialect (refines: Russian-influenced tendency to stress long vowels); Novikova & Sem 1997 state word stress is 'unclear, not experimentally studied'; Petrova 1967 has no stress section. Nothing contradicts the weight-sensitive right-edge coding (peak on final syllable if CVV/CVC, else penult; non-phonemic pitch accent).

sources.quote: 'As in the Southern dialect, an accent by pitch (high-low accent) is recognised. In every word (phrase) the position and pattern of the accent is fixed and non-distinctive (Tsumagari 1983, Tsumagari 2009). The second mora from the end of the word (if that is a secondary mora, the preceding primary mora) is pronounced high and is the accent peak (Tsumagari 2009: 3-4); except in two-mora words whose first mora is high, the stretch from the word's second mora to the peak is high (ibid.). sources.note: Glottolog's top-ranked 'grammar' entry; now checked: sec. 2.1.2 says word stress is 'unclear, not studied experimentally' — documents that the Russian tradition offers no competing rule.
